summary: Lists requirements for a Kerberos-based way to negotiate keys on the Internet, aiming at a protocol that is fast, easy to manage, and cryptographically sound without needing public key infrastructure.

eli5.summary: It describes what is needed for a quick way to agree on a secret handshake using a trusted helper rather than complicated locks.

subtitle: Using a trusted server instead of peer-to-peer to negotiate secure connections

tldr.problem: IKE requires expensive cryptographic operations (Diffie-Hellman and X.509 signatures) on every peer, and managing symmetric keys between all peers creates an O(n^2) scaling problem.
tldr.mechanism: KINK leverages Kerberos, which uses a trusted Key Distribution Center to issue session keys. Peers authenticate via Kerberos tickets instead of doing direct peer-to-peer authentication.
tldr.outcome: A faster, simpler protocol for establishing IPsec security associations in environments with a central authentication server. It does not replace IKE but offers a better choice when a trusted third party is available.

facts.label: Key distribution complexity
facts.value: O(n) for symmetric keys, not O(n^2)

today: RFC 3129 is an Informational RFC. It specifies requirements for the KINK protocol, which was later defined in RFC 4430.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
KINK stands for Kerberized Internet Negotiation of Keys. This RFC lists the requirements for a new protocol that uses Kerberos to negotiate IPsec security associations, an alternative to the existing IKE (Internet Key Exchange) protocol.

Unlike IKE, which requires two peers to authenticate directly to each other, KINK assumes a trusted third party (a Key Distribution Center, or KDC) that both peers trust. The peers use Kerberos tickets issued by the KDC to prove their identity, rather than using expensive cryptographic operations like Diffie-Hellman or X.509 certificates on the peers themselves.
sections.eli5: KINK is a way for two computers to agree on a secret and trust each other, by asking a trusted school secretary instead of having to verify each other directly.

sections.title: Why a New Protocol Is Needed
sections.content:
IKE, defined in RFC 2409, is a peer-to-peer protocol. Each peer must understand the site's security policy and perform expensive operations: Diffie-Hellman key exchange (computationally expensive and vulnerable to denial of service) and X.509 certificate signatures (also expensive to compute and hard to deploy at scale). Managing symmetric keys between all peers is an O(n^2) problem: with 100 peers, you need 4,950 different keys.

Kerberos solves these problems by centralizing authentication. The KDC does the expensive work once, then issues a session key to both peers. Peers authenticate using symmetric keys (O(n) keys for n peers, all stored in the KDC) or certificates, but the expensive DH and certificate operations happen at the KDC, not on the peers. Security policy is also centralized, rather than trusting each peer to enforce it correctly.
sections.eli5: IKE makes each computer prove itself to every other computer it talks to, which is slow and needs lots of secret keys. Kerberos has a central office that vouches for everyone, so computers can trust each other much faster.

sections.title: Core Design Principles
sections.content:
KINK uses Kerberos session keys found in Kerberos tickets as the basis for IPsec security association keys. This means once a peer obtains a Kerberos ticket from the KDC, it has everything needed to establish IPsec security associations without further interaction with the KDC (as long as the ticket is still valid).

The protocol must support both Kerberos symmetric-key authentication and Kerberos PKinit (public-key initial authentication). It must also support Kerberos User-to-User mode, a feature that allows two peers to authenticate using shared tickets when one or both cannot obtain a direct service ticket from the KDC.

KINK is not a replacement for IKE. The key difference: IKE allows two peers to mutually authenticate without any third party, while KINK requires an actively participating KDC. However, in many deployments, having a trusted third party is desirable because it simplifies key distribution and policy management.
sections.eli5: KINK gives peers a ticket from the KDC that acts like a magic key: they can use the ticket to set up secure connections without asking the KDC again. It works even when peers are in different authentication groups (realms).

sections.title: What KINK Must Do
sections.content:
The protocol must support creating, modifying, rekeying and deleting IPsec security associations. It must integrate into the IPsec architecture (RFC 2401) and be able to set up both transport and tunnel modes, as well as both AH (Authentication Header) and ESP (Encapsulating Security Payload) security associations.

Either peer can be the initiator or responder, regardless of whether it is a Kerberos client (holding only a Ticket-Granting Ticket) or a Kerberos server (with a keytab). The protocol must handle multiple Kerberos realms gracefully and be resilient to absolute time skew (when one machine's clock is off). It must be able to rekey security associations without the KDC's help if the Kerberos session ticket is still valid.

The protocol must negotiate cipher suites, set up IPsec flow selectors (which traffic to protect), and mitigate third-party denial-of-service attacks (so-called zombie attacks). It must support both IPv4 and IPv6, and be general enough to be used for more than just IPsec keying.
sections.eli5: KINK must let either peer start a secure connection, handle multiple trusted servers, work when clocks are a little wrong, and be ready for IPv4 and IPv6.

sections.title: Security Inheritance
sections.content:
Security associations created by KINK will inherit the union of IPsec and Kerberos's existing security properties and weaknesses. The requirements do not mandate addressing those weaknesses unless a combination creates a new weakness unique to KINK.

The protocol must be cryptographically sound without requiring public key infrastructure. However, it can optionally use Kerberos PKinit to leverage X.509 certificates for initial client authentication, amortizing the cost of certificate operations over the lifetime of the credentials.
sections.eli5: KINK is as safe as Kerberos and IPsec are. It does not add new security holes, but it also does not fix old ones.
